3099.prule: One strong stress per word on the first syllable of the root morpheme; syllables of prefixes before the root and of suffixes after it are unstressed. In an unprefixed word the stressed root-initial syllable is word-initial; with one or more prefix syllables the stress sits on the root, i.e. its position is set by morpheme class (root vs. affix), not by syllable count or weight.
3099.srule: Optional, light secondary stress on the second syllable before and the second syllable after the root-initial (primary-stressed) syllable, e.g. zàphàni 'straw' ['zàphà″ní]; 'sometimes heard', and 'not strong enough to be confused with the stress which signals a root-initial juncture'.

3100.prule: No Temuan-specific stress rule is reachable. 3104.tone: Three contrasting level tones H/M/L (Tench 2007: 232; Newman 1964: 35 'three basic tones', fn. 7 'Three tonemes are necessary and sufficient for marking lexical items'); no contour tones even on long/diphthongal vowels; tone is lexically contrastive (Tench's minimal pairs vi 'to enter' M vs vi 'iron' L, zhum 'warthog' M vs zhum 'dark' L; grammatical contrast present progressive á vs present perfect a); mid tone partially assimilates to a neighbouring H or L; disyllables lack HL and LH; voiced obstruents tentatively favour L. Tone in discourse / longer utterances explicitly not yet analysed by either author. On stress/accent both sources are silent: in Tench 2007 'accent(s)' occurs only in the dialect sense ('Zambuk accent', 'some Tera accents, e.g. Difa') and 'prominently' only of a sign on the Deba town gate; 'stress' does not occur. 3105.prule: Primary accent is lexically specified ('livre', 'já previamente definido no léxico', 'a posição do acento primário já vem marcada na forma subjacente') and falls on one of the first three syllables of the word (left-edge three-syllable window); its position is not phonologically predictable and is quantity-insensitive (syllabic trochees, 'insensível ao peso silábico'). The final syllable is normally extrametrical. Secondary prominence: from the lexically marked primary, left-headed binary feet are built bidirectionally, no degenerate feet, leftover final syllable extrametrical (§4.6.5).
3105.srule: Metrical analysis only (Martins 2009 §4.6.5): from the lexically placed primary accent, left-headed binary feet (syllabic trochees) are built bidirectionally toward both word edges, degenerate feet forbidden, a leftover final syllable extrametrical, so foot-head prominence falls on alternate syllables counted from the primary; the author does not call these secondary stresses, transcribes only the primary accent in output forms, and gives no phonetic evidence. Silva 2009 states that most words carry a primary and a secondary accent but gives no placement.

evidence_works.detail: States the same system the entry codes from Martins 2009: two accent types, acute (more force, higher pitch, following consonant lengthened) and circumflex (more force, falling pitch, vowel lengthened); every verb has two fundamental accent positions ('primeira' and 'segunda' posição) and verbs fall into three classes by the pair of positions, 1-2, 2-3 or 1-3 (Nota 1: 'Existem três padrões de intensidade, e segundo um ou outro deles os verbos podem ser classificados de verbo 1-2, verbo 2-3 ou verbo 1-3'), which is the record's '2/3 – 1/3 – 1/2' interaction with root classes. Adds detail the record does not carry: (a) the final syllable is 'uma posição não permitida aos acentos agudos', so a short stem reduplicates the vowel of -ne to keep the acute off the last syllable (Nota 22); (b) 'Quando um acento agudo fundamental se desloca até a sílaba imediata, torna-se circunflexo; se deslocado mais uma sílaba ainda, permanece agudo' (Nota 1); (c) the grammatical load of the two positions: first-position accent marks objective (or locative) emphasis and the imperative, second-position accent marks subjective emphasis, the conditional and temporal clauses (Apêndice 2: 'A intensidade de primeira posição marca ênfase objetiva ou, no caso de verbos de movimento, ênfase locativa. A intensidade de segunda posição marca ênfase subjetiva'; §1.2.1.1: imperative vs conditional 'distinguindo-se uma da outra por posição acentual'). The two 'posições de intensidade' are alternative placements of the single word accent, not a second stress, so nothing here bears on sec_status.

3106.tone: Oakes: Proto-Chibchan was tonal; Heinze (1980) analyzed Teribe as tonal with two tonemes, but 'the tonal system has faded away and been replaced for the most part with a system of contrastive stress'. Vestiges: H vs L contrast in colour terms and reduplicated adjectives (low tone = 'somewhat'), only three genuine tone minimal pairs, monosyllabic nouns whose underlying tone surfaces on an attached enclitic or perturbs sentence intonation (shiy 'older brother' always high); younger speakers have lost the pitch distinctions. tn.translation: Tetela has two tonemes: a level high and a level low toneme. These tonemes can be attached to vowels and also to long consonants. 3108.dq: l’accent, en tetserret, est restreint aux frontières du nom. En effet, en tetserret, l’accent d’un nom bisyllabique ne se déplace jamais sur les éléments précédant le nominal, même s’il s’agit de masculins qui ont tendance à être accentués sur la syllabe antépénulitème (p. 267; contrasted with Tamasheq, where the antepenult rule applies over the accentual group / noun phrase, table 83 p. 290 'Dom…
3108.prule: Word accent placed by grammatical category, not by a fixed edge, weight or lexical marking. Nouns in isolation: masculine nouns accented by default on the antepenult (penult when disyllabic; when a plural suffix adds a syllable the accent moves back to the new antepenult: ˈeylim / ˈiləm-an), feminine nouns on the penult at any length (t-ənəˈʃkəfaṛ-t / t-ənəʃkəˈfaṛ-in). Verbs: aorist/imperative on the first syllable of the verb (preverbal particles d-/ar/har attract the accent), perfective on the final syllable (for long/geminate verbs on the vowel after the first consonant), imperfective on the first vowel of the stem, negative perfective (wər + PFV) on the first syllable of the verb including the subject prefix.

3111.tone: Three tone levels H, M, L, with M restricted in nouns to HM sequences; lexical noun melodies /H HL HM LH HLH LHL LHM/; contours HL, HM, LH, rarely LHL; verbs show tonal and segmental ablaut; tone sandhi (2.7.3) and possessive {L} overlay after dí. The grammar neither posits nor explicitly denies word stress/accent for Tiefo-N: it has no stress/accent section, 'accent' does not occur anywhere, and the single 'stress' token (p. 30) is a phonetic remark about a 'stress-like pulse' that creates a weak syllable break in prolonged long vowels of plurals, not a claim about a stress system. (The sister-language grammar Heath & Ouattara 2021 says of Tiefo-D 'There is no evidence in favor of an accentual interpretation of tones'; no such sentence exists for Tiefo-N and the 2021 grammar does not extend it to Tiefo-N.)

tn.quote: Tiefo-N too has three tone levels, but they pattern differently. Whereas W98 reports many M-toned nouns for Tiefo-D, Tiefo-N has none (except in HM-toned stems). ... Contoured tones within a syllable in Tiefo-N are limited to two falling contours (<HL> and <HM>), one rising contour <LH>, and (rarely) a bell-shaped contour <LHL>. ... There are three tone levels: H, M, and L. ... Slashes /…/ enclose lexical tone melodies. Monosyllabic Tiefo-N nouns may be /H/, /HL/, /HM/, and /LH/. Nonmonosyllabics may be any of these, plus /HLH/, /LHL/, or /LHM/. There is no pure /M/ melody for noun stems.

tn.quote: Stress in Tigrinya has no phonological value and easily shifts from one syllable to another. Dynamic stress is very weak and sometimes almost imperceptible. … Pitch is an important element of the Tigrinya stress pattern, but it is also rather unstable. Dynamic stress and pitch may not coincide: ndbdrd ‘to be’ (“ — high pitch; ~ — dynamic stress). Sentence intonation is clearly predominant over the stress of an individual word, The relationship between these two features requires further investigation, but it is clear that rhythmical units very often do not coincide with single words.
tn.cite: Kogan, Leonid E. 1997. Tigrinya. In Robert Hetzron (ed.), The Semitic Languages, 424-445. London: Routledge.
tn.note: No tone inventory is described: pitch is an unstable element of a weak, non-phonemic stress and may fall on another syllable; sentence intonation predominates; the relation needs further study.

3112.cfw: Kogan 1997 and Bulakh & Kogan 2013 describe Tigrinya word stress as weak, non-phonological and overridden by phrase intonation, Leslau 1941's fieldwork and Buckley 1997 say the same, and the only placement rules to the contrary are nineteenth-century ones (Praetorius 1871, Schreiber 1887, De Vito 1895) that rest on other people's transcriptions and contradict one another, though Bulakh & Kogan 2013 admit the prosody has never been systematically studied. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Kogan 1997 1997.

3113.prule: No fixed stress position. Stress is weak, dynamic and mobile; its place is 'not fixed and does not depend on the phonetic make-up of the word' but is tied to semantics or syllable count, and place and strong/weak intensity are both contrastive (minimal pairs by place рáзи 'handful' vs разú 'in agreement', къáчIи 'cocoon' vs къачIú 'on time'; by intensity къáру 'boot-top' vs къàру 'time'). Statistical default is initial: the overwhelming majority of native disyllabic nouns and most verbs are stressed on the first syllable, but a set of di- and polysyllabic nouns is stressed on the second (айáр, бег’áр, бесýн) and the author states she could not find the regularity governing stress shift in noun inflection.
3113.srule: Not mentioned in Magomedova 2014 (pp. 106-109, whole article read): one stress per example word throughout; the strong (á) vs weak (à) contrast is a distinctive intensity grade of the single word stress ('На первом слоге ударение может быть разной интенсивности (сильное – слабое)'), not a secondary stress. Borise 2020 sec. 6.2 and Magomedbekova 1999 sec. 2.1.2 are likewise silent.

3113.tone: No tone or pitch accent described. The source posits a contrastive 'correlation of intensity - non-intensity' of stress: on the first syllable stress may be strong (á) or weak (à), on later syllables usually strong, and the strong/weak contrast is distinctive (къáру 'boot-top' - къàру 'time'; áра 'ear of grain' - àри 'here'). Borise (2020, second-hand summary held) mentions an attempted tonal reanalysis of this strong/weak contrast in a companion chapter; not adopted here since both first-hand descriptions call it ударение (stress).

3114.dq: এই ঝোঁক ইংরাজী কিংবা বাংলা ভাষার শ্বাসাঘাতের মতো নয়। ইংরাজী ভাষায় প্রত্যেক মূল শব্দের নিজস্ব শ্বাসাঘাত আছে ... তিপ্রা ভাষার বাক্প্রবাহে শ্বাসাঘাত পড়ে দু'ভাবে। (The stress is set in the speech flow / breath group and expressly contrasted with English per-word stress; clause (a) is word-specific lexical marking, clause (b) breath-group-final.)
3114.dloc: Phonology chapter, p. 16 (archive.org leaf 28); tone discussion pp. 14-15 (leaf 27).
3114.prule: No word-stress rule. The source describes a tone system (four pitch contours diagrammed, word meaning 'sometimes' depends on tone, minimal pairs butui 'broth' rising vs butui 'egg' falling, mairung, chaklai) plus a stress (ঝোঁক/শ্বাসাঘাত) that is explicitly unlike English per-word stress or Bengali word-initial stress: in connected speech stress falls (a) word-initially on particular lexical items to keep near-homophones apart (bútui 'egg' vs butui 'broth'), and (b) on the final vowel of a breath group when that vowel is a verbal tense suffix, case ending or particle.
3114.srule: Not mentioned in Chakraborty 1981, ch. 1 Phonology (ধ্বনিতত্ত্ব) pp. 14-16 (tone and stress discussion read in full): the only stress placements given are the lexical word-initial stress on particular words and the breath-group-final stress on a tense suffix, case ending or particle; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described.

3115.prule: Every word carries exactly one of two lexical tones (high level or falling), docked on a lexically determined syllable that may be any syllable of the word (four patterns on disyllables, six on trisyllables). Syllables before the tone are mid/neutral in pitch; the tone spreads rightward to the end of the word. Tone position is contrastive, not positional. No stress rule is stated; the authors consider an accent-plus-tone analysis ('the tone is attracted to the accented syllable') and decline it as an unneeded complication.

It proved more revealing, however, to consider the tone to be a feature of the entire word, while recognizing that either tone can occur on either the first or the second syllable. This is reminiscent of the pattern of pitch-accent languages such as Japanese, where the pitch contour varies according to the location of accent (McCawley 1978) and, for that matter, it recalls the pattern of English stress, which can fall…

3115.idn: Tiwa (formerly 'Lalung'), Bodo subgroup of Tibeto-Burman, 'spoken further to the east, mostly south of the river' (Brahmaputra, Assam); data from Umswai, Karbi Anglong district (Hill Tiwa) per the authors' affiliation and the 2006 preface; data: Joseph and Burling worked on the Tiwa tone system together in April 1999…
3115.tone: Two-tone system (high level vs falling), one tone per word, culminative, on a lexically free syllable; described against Japanese pitch accent and English stress. p. 49: 'It would be possible to describe Tiwa as being characterized by accent as well as tone, and to say that the tone is attracted to the accented syllable. This seems only to introduce an extra and unneeded complication'. p. 50: 'All syllables before the position of the tone are mid or neutral in pitch... Either a high tone or a falling tone spreads to all the syllables that follow.' Joseph & Burling 2006 (CIIL monograph, ch. 1, pp. 8-12, archive.org) restate it: 'Polysyllabic words take just one tone for the entire word, but the tone can occur on any syllable' (p. 8); in echo constructions the toned syllables have 'higher pitches and perhaps a bit more stress' (p. 10), the only mention of stress as a correlate; the first- vs second-syllable falling contrast has low functional load and even literate native speakers mark it inconsistently (pp. 9-10). Dawson 2020 (UC Berkeley diss., p. 10-11): tones 'associated with a particular syllable in the word, and spread left-to-right', no stress statement.

3116.tone: Lexical tone language with a positional stress statement. Thelin 1980 p.5 sec. 3: 'A syllable may be either ballistic (marked by an acute accent over the nuclear vowel) or controlled (unmarked). The primary feature which distinguishes ballistic syllables versus controlled syllables in all environments is that the ballistic syllable ends in a crescendo or an extra pulse, whereas the controlled syllable has a decrescendo or at least lack of crescendo.'... 'There are four simple tones: very high /1/, high /2/, mid /3/ and low /4/, and three tone sequences: one upglide /42/ and two downglides /12, 34/.' (both sentences). Thelin p.1 calls the ballistic feature 'ballistic stress' in the syllable formula ('two tones or one tone and ballistic stress'); it is a property of the stressed syllable, not the word-stress position. Unstressed (pretonic) syllables also carry the four level tones (L&R sec. 8.3) but only the sequence 34 and never the ballistic accent.

3117.prule: Primary stress on the final syllable of the morphological stem (root + derivation/compounding): word-final in non-verbs; in verbs stem-final, with all inflectional suffixes (INV, PL, PERF, INDEP/DEP) and enclitics unstressed, so verb stress is also word-final when the inflection is only consonantal (most cases) and falls on the penult, antepenult or pre-antepenult when one to three suffix syllables follow the stem (126-127). Prefixes never affect placement; compounds stress the last syllable of the second root. Lyon 1980 (Tlahuitoltepec proper): the tonic syllable is the root syllable, except certain verbal suffixes that are always tonic.
3117.srule: At most one secondary stress per word, at a word edge: in a trisyllabic (suffixless) word the first syllable has secondary and the last primary stress ([ˌnɨ.tɨ.ɡɨːk] 'third', compound [ˌtɤɤ.ɰɨ.det] 'to go sell'); if the third syllable is a suffix, primary on the second syllable and no secondary ([a.mɨh.kɨp]); when two or three suffix syllables follow the verb stem, stem-final primary plus secondary on the word-final syllable ([tɨh.kɨ.ˌdɨp] 'they enter', [a.mɨh.kɨ.ɲɨ.ˌdɨp]); noun plural mëjä'äy-tëjk [mɨ.ˌhʌʌ.dʲɨʰk] has secondary on the penult next to the stressed suffix (fn. 13, 'somehow anomalous'). Author adds that other Mixe languages seem to show 'a competition between the first and the last syllable'.

tn.quote: James (2003) analyses the role of tone in the organisation of grammatical morphemes in a number of the subsystems of TobC. 3123.prule: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word (stem plus suffixes); weight plays no role. The Tialo paragogic vowel E, added after almost every consonant-final word, and enclitics/free possessor forms are outside the stress domain, so a consonant-final root pronounced with E surfaces with antepenultimate stress (['uŋkule] = 'ungkul + E) while the root itself keeps penultimate stress.
3123.srule: Only in reduplication: the reduplicated syllable of accented (C)CV-reduplication (RDP1) is distinctly lengthened and is what the source calls 'secondary stress', written with a grave accent (mensìnsiing 'rather wet', menìnimpis 'rather narrow'; speakers vary in how strongly it is stressed). Rhythmic secondary stress in unreduplicated words: not mentioned in Himmelmann 2001, secs 3.4.7-3.4.8, 3.5.9-3.5.10, 3.7 (pp.72-73, 81, 91-92 read).

tn.quote: Like all other Dogon languages, Tɔmmɔ-Sɔ is tonal, with tonal primitives H[igh] and L[ow], marked {v́} and {v̀}, respectively. It also has two contour tones, <LH> rising ({v̌} or {v̀v́}) and <HL> falling ({v̂} or {v́v̀}), though instances of the latter are rare. ... Every stem must have at least one H ... Tɔmmɔ-Sɔ has two tonal primitives, H[igh] and L[ow], which can combine to make two contour tones: HL (falling) and LH (rising). Each tonal component must be mapped to a mora; thus, no short (monomoraic) syllable may be pronounced with a contour tone.

3125.prule: No word-stress rule is stated.
